introduction: The Caribbean History School-Based Assessment is a research project on a historical topic of your choice, based on primary and secondary sources. It rewards a clear question, evidence that is used rather than copied, and a judgement of your own. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the exact requirements and marks for your examination session.

tasks.title: Research Question
tasks.explanation: State the question your project will answer and why it is historically significant.

tasks.title: Aims
tasks.explanation: List two or three specific objectives that the research will achieve.

tasks.title: Methods
tasks.explanation: Explain how you will gather evidence: which archives, libraries, newspapers, oral testimonies or interviews.

tasks.title: Sources
tasks.explanation: Present your evidence - extracts, photographs, tables, summaries of interviews - with the source of each item recorded.

tasks.title: Analysis
tasks.explanation: Interpret the evidence: what does it show, whose viewpoint does it represent, and how reliable is it?

tasks.title: Findings
tasks.explanation: State your conclusions, answer your research question, and note what further research would help.

sampleTitle: How did the 1938 labour disturbances in Jamaica change the relationship between workers and the colonial government?

sample.body: This project examines why the 1938 unrest on the Kingston waterfront produced permanent trade unions and political parties, while earlier strikes had not.
sample.tips: Keep the question narrow enough to answer with the sources you can reach.

sample.body: The Moyne Report (1939) states that wages on the waterfront were insufficient for a family to live on. Read against the newspaper reports of the strike, this shows that the commission's evidence confirmed what workers had already said in public - the argument was not only about wages but about who had the right to be heard.
sample.tips: Quote the source briefly, then explain what it shows and how far it can be trusted.

marking: Marks reward a clear research question, evidence drawn from identified sources, analysis rather than narration, awareness of bias and viewpoint, and a supported conclusion. Copied extracts without comment earn little.
checklist: Analysis shows use of evidence, not just narration
Viewpoint and reliability of sources discussed

categories.comment: The question is one sentence, about one relationship over one period, and it is argued into significance: it covers the origin of the unions and parties that governed Jamaica after 1944, it is answerable with libraries a Jamaican student can reach, and every term in it - the disturbances, workers, the colonial government, the relationship - is defined in section 3 before the research starts.

Four objectives, each naming the evidence it needs before the research begins, covering the position before 1938, the government's response, the test of who held which powers in 1944, and the attempt to recover what workers themselves wanted. The third objective is drawn so that it can give an unwelcome answer, which is what an objective is for.

A six-step plan week by week with the archives, libraries and people used; 12 sources each described by type, location, what it can and cannot show and its reliability; six tests applied to every claim of fact; and the limitations stated plainly, including second-hand use of the CO 137 despatches, the silence of the record on workers' own voices, and the ethics of recording a family memory.

Four pages of evidence: a 10-entry chronology from Frome to the 1944 election, each entry with its place and source; 9 extracts in the four-column note-card form, with real sources summarised and cited and the invented ones labelled; the four local sources given with their evidential status; and the legal and official record from the Trade Union Law of 1919 to the 1944 election, including what each measure did not do.

Five pages of analysis rather than narration: the baseline relationship before 1938, what changed in 1938 and how quickly, the viewpoint and interest of every source, the remembered wage tested and rejected as proof, and the argument weighed in two halves - method changed quickly, power distribution slowly - with the evidence for and against each claim set out side by side.

Six findings, each with its evidence and a confidence rating that admits the weakest; four open questions with the sources that would settle them; and four recommendations that can actually be carried out, including recording the memories of those who were children in 1938 before they are lost, digitising the 1938 press, and quoting the language of 1938 rather than borrowing it.

pages.heading: Cover page, note on sources and contents
pages.body: This is a research project for the Caribbean History School-Based Assessment. It asks one question: How did the 1938 labour disturbances in Jamaica change the relationship between workers and the colonial government? The period examined runs from the stoppage on the West Indies Sugar Company estate at Frome in May 1938 to the general election of December 1944 under the new constitution, because by then the party that had grown out of the 1938 union was forming the government. A note on sources comes before everything else, because in a history project the honesty of the evidence is the argument. The events, the dates, the legislation and the real sources named in this report - the Daily Gleaner of 1938, the Moyne Commission's report Cmd. 6607, the Colonial Office despatches in the CO 137 series, the Trade Union Law 1919, the 1944 constitution and election, and the secondary works by Post, Munroe and Hart - are genuine and can be checked. Extracts from those real sources are given as my summaries of what they say, with the source and date, and not as invented quotations: I worked from notes taken in the library, and a project that manufactures wording and then calls it a quotation has destroyed its own evidence. Four local sources are different: the interview with the candidate's great-grandmother, the estate timekeeper's memoir, the 1939 school magazine and the 1938 letter to the editor are all INVENTED for this worked example, and they are labelled INVENTED everywhere they appear. They are included because a real project of this kind would have such material, and because they let the report show how oral and private evidence is tested rather than believed. The candidate, the centre, the family and the school are invented; the history is not.

pages.heading: Statement of the problem: the question and why it matters
pages.body: The question is: How did the 1938 labour disturbances in Jamaica change the relationship between workers and the colonial government? It is worth asking because 1938 is the point at which the British Caribbean stopped being governed as if labour had no politics. Before that year, a worker with a grievance on a Jamaican sugar estate had the law's permission to combine and no way to be heard: no employer had to meet a union, and the government treated a wage dispute as a matter for the police. Within six years of the disturbances there was universal adult suffrage, an elected House of Representatives, and a Chief Minister's party that had begun as a trade union. Something large happened in between, and the interesting historical question is what exactly it was. The question matters for three reasons. First, it tests a claim that Jamaicans often make about 1938, that the year changed everything: my evidence shows that it changed the method of government quickly and the distribution of power slowly. Second, it is a case study in how official power responds to pressure - first with force, then with an inquiry, then with administration, then with the vote. Third, it can be answered with the sources a school student in Jamaica can actually reach, which matters, because a research question that needs a flight to London is not a research question for this project.

table.caption: Why this question was chosen, and what makes it answerable
rows: Is it narrow enough to answer?
It asks one thing about one relationship - workers and the colonial government - over one period of six years, not a history of the disturbances
Is there evidence in reach?
The 8 real sources listed in section 6 are all available in Jamaica, in the National Library's newspaper microfilm, a reference library, the school library and two published secondary works
Is it historically significant?
It covers the origins of the trade unions and parties that governed Jamaica after 1944, and the beginning of the process that ended in independence in 1962
Is it arguable rather than obvious?
Yes: the government's method changed quickly while the ownership of the sugar industry and the level of wages did not, so the answer is a matter of judgement, not of fact
Does it let the workers appear?
Only partly, and the project says so: the official record is rich on what was done to workers and poor on what workers themselves said

pages.heading: Statement of the problem: scope, key terms and what is left out
pages.body: Every term in the question is fixed before the research begins, so that the answer cannot drift to whatever the sources happen to say. The disturbances of 1938 are the wave of stoppages, marches and confrontations that began with the stoppage at Frome in May 1938 and spread through the cane parishes and to Kingston, with the deaths at Frome and the police action of late May as their most violent moments. Workers means those who worked for wages with their hands, on the estates, in the docks and in the towns, and not smallholders, who appear in the record only as a class that was frightened of what the strike might cost. The colonial government means the Governor, his officials and the Legislative Council: the people who in 1938 could deploy the police and could not be voted out. The relationship between them is measured in three ways and no others: the law, meaning what the statute allowed workers and unions to do; administration, meaning whether the government had any machinery for dealing with labour except force; and politics, meaning whether workers had a voice with power behind it. Two deliberate limits keep the project honest. The first is geographical: the 1937 disturbances in Barbados and Trinidad are referred to only as background, because the project's evidence base is Jamaican. The second is chronological: the report stops at the end of 1944, so it does not attempt the story of the 1945-62 period, in which the same relationship was worked out again in different conditions.

table.caption: Key terms defined, and the limits accepted
rows: The disturbances of 1938
The stoppages and confrontations from the Frome stoppage of May 1938 through the sugar parishes and the Kingston waterfront, and the unrest into June
Workers
People who worked for wages - estate labourers, dock workers, urban wage earners - and not smallholders or the middle class
The colonial government
The Governor, the colonial officials and the Legislative Council, with the Colonial Office in London above them
The relationship, measured in three ways
1. the law; 2. administrative machinery for labour; 3. political voice and its results at the polls
Geographical limit
Jamaica only, with the 1937 disturbances in Barbados and Trinidad used as background
Chronological limit
From May 1938 to the general election of December 1944; the years after 1944 are outside the project
What is left out
The full history of the sugar industry, the details of union factional politics, and the story after 1944, each of which would need its own project

pages.heading: Aims and objectives, and how each one would be met
pages.body: The aim of the project is to decide, on evidence, how far the relationship between workers and the colonial government changed between the disturbances of May 1938 and the election of December 1944. Three objectives together achieve that aim, and each was written so that it names the evidence it needs before the research started. The first is to establish the position before 1938, using the law on unions and whatever the officials of the time wrote about how they dealt with labour. The second is to trace what the government did in response to the disturbances, which means separating what it said from what it did: the police, the arrests, the commission, the labour office, the constitution. The third is to test the extent of the change by asking who held which powers in 1944 - and this is the objective that disciplines the answer, because it forbids the easy conclusion that everything changed when the franchise did. The third objective is deliberately the one most likely to give an unwelcome answer, since the sources that show the vote being won are the same sources that show the sugar industry and the wages untouched.

table.caption: Objectives and the evidence each one requires
rows: 1. To establish the relationship before 1938
The legal position of unions before the disturbances, and officials' own account of how they handled labour disputes
Trade Union Law 1919; CO 137 despatches as quoted in Post (1978)
Provides the baseline the change is measured against in section 13
2. To trace the government's response, 1938 to 1940
The sequence of force, inquiry and administration, with dates
Daily Gleaner 1938; Cmd. 6607; Post (1978); Hart (1999)
Shows how quickly the method of government changed, in section 14
3. To test who held which powers in 1944
The constitution of 1944, the election result, and what the elected ministers could decide about wages and the industry
1944 constitution and election record; Munroe (1972)
Decides how far the change went, in sections 17 and 18
4. To recover, so far as the evidence allows, what workers wanted and said
Any account in which a worker speaks, and an honest note of where the record is silent
The 4 INVENTED local sources, kept clearly apart from the real ones, plus the silences in the real record
Keeps the project from answering only from the government's side, and becomes a finding in its own right

pages.heading: Method of investigation: the plan of research
pages.body: The research ran in five steps over seven weeks. The first step was to read the question into the sources, which meant going to the National Library of Jamaica and reading the Daily Gleaner on microfilm for the months of May to October 1938, taking notes by date and copying the wording of any public statement of the government or the estate owners. The second step was to read the official side of the same events in the report of the West India Royal Commission, Cmd. 6607, and in the despatches quoted at length in Post's Arise Ye Starvelings, so that the government's reasoning could be read in its own words rather than through a historian's summary. The third step was to talk to people. One interview was recorded, with my great-grandmother, who was born in 1930; the questions were prepared in advance, asked without leading her, and written up the same evening. A typed memoir lent by another family and a 1939 school magazine were photographed in the school archive. The fourth step was to establish the law and the constitutional position from the Trade Union Law 1919, the 1944 constitution and the election results, using Munroe for the detail of how the 1944 constitution actually worked. The fifth step was to write, and then to go back through every claim with the tests in section 7 and mark what could not be supported. Two things shaped the plan more than anything else. The first is that the newspaper and the commission describe the same months, which allows one to be checked against the other. The second is that the people whose lives changed are the hardest to hear, so the plan had to find a way of saying what could not be known, rather than filling the gap with what a textbook says they must have felt.

pages.heading: Method: the sources and what each can and cannot show
pages.body: The project uses 12 sources: 9 primary and 3 secondary. Of the 12, 8 are real and can be checked by anyone with access to a library, and 4 are INVENTED for this worked example to stand in for the local material a student can collect. Every source is set out below with what it can show, what it cannot, and how far it can be trusted, before a single claim is built on it. Two decisions came out of making this table. The first is that the Moyne report is the strongest single document in the project, because it is the government's own commission confirming the workers' central complaint that wages would not feed a family - evidence from the other side is worth more than evidence from a sympathetic one. The second is that the newspaper is more useful for language than for fact: reading the Gleaner of May 1938 photographs the vocabulary of the time, in which a wage claim became an 'agitation' and a stoppage became an 'unpleasantness', and that vocabulary is part of what the project is describing. Nothing in the analysis rests on a source whose weaknesses are not written down here.

pages.heading: Method: how the evidence was recorded, tested and weighed
pages.body: Evidence was recorded in one way throughout, so that the notes could be used afterwards. Every item was written on a card with four headings: what it says; who wrote it and when; what that writer wanted; and where I found it, with the date of the issue or the page. The cards were then kept in two boxes, written-during-the-period and written-later, because the Moyne report published in 1945 and a memory recorded in 2026 cannot be weighed in the same way as a newspaper published on the morning after the shooting. Six tests were applied to every claim used in the analysis, and they are in the table below. The tests did real work rather than decorating the project. Apply the fifth test - whose voice is missing - to almost any page of the official record and the answer is: the worker's, and very often the woman's, which is why the analysis in section 15 ends up treating what the record leaves out as a finding rather than a gap. Apply the third test - can a second independent source be found - to the claim that Bustamante was detained and then released within days, and it holds, because the press and the despatches as quoted by Post agree. Apply it to the remembered wage of about two shillings a day and it fails: that figure appears in this project in one place only, in a family memory, and section 16 therefore treats it as unproven rather than repeating it as a fact.

table.caption: The six tests applied to every claim of fact
rows: Who wrote it, and what did they want?
Every source is described by its author's interest before it is used: planter, official, editor, missionary, worker, historian
Was it written at the time?
Sources written during 1938-39 are separated from sources written later, including the 1945 publication of the Moyne report and the memories recorded for this project
Can a second, independent source be found?
Every claim used in the analysis appears in at least two of the sources listed, or is marked as resting on one source only
Does a source that disagrees exist, and what does it say?
The estate owners' case and the newspaper's hostility to the strikers are kept in the report rather than left out
Whose voice is missing?
Asked of every page: workers, women and cane farmers are almost absent from the official record, which is itself a finding
Is the language of the source borrowed by accident?
Words from 1938 such as 'agitator' and 'unpleasantness' are kept in quotation marks, so that the source's vocabulary is not silently adopted

pages.heading: Method: limitations, the missing voices and the ethics of the interview
pages.body: The limitations are stated plainly because a project that hides them is asking to be believed rather than read. The first is access. The Colonial Office despatches in the CO 137 series are held in London, so they were read at second hand in Post's book, which means that the selection of those documents was made by a historian and not by me; this is a real limit and the despatches are used only for the government's reasoning, never for a fact that depends on the document as a whole. The second is the record's silence: there is no diary, letter or testimony from an estate labourer in 1938 in any source I could reach, so the workers' own account of their aims cannot be recovered from the real evidence, and the 4 invented local sources in this sample exist to show how such material would be handled if a student had it. The third is the newspaper: one paper, from one class, in a period when most workers could not read it. The fourth is the interview. Recording a family memory about 1938 raises questions a project must answer rather than avoid: my great-grandmother agreed to be recorded and to have the recording kept with the project, she was told what it was for, she was asked open questions and not told what answer was wanted, and she was shown the written-up notes afterwards. Two rules governed its use. She is never quoted on anything she could not have known at eight years old, and nothing she remembers is used as proof of a fact that the written record does not already establish. In this sample that second rule is the whole reason section 16 exists: the wage figure she remembers is examined and left unproven, and the sentence that carries the argument is about dignity, which is a subject on which memory is evidence in its own right.
bullets: Access: the CO 137 despatches were read only as quoted in Post (1978), so a historian chose which of them I saw
Silence in the record: no worker's own diary, letter or testimony from 1938 was available; the four local sources that carry that voice are INVENTED and labelled
One newspaper only: the Daily Gleaner spoke for a literate middle class and its editorials were hostile to the strikers
The official record is also the most complete record, so there is a constant pull towards telling the story from the government's side
The interview: consent obtained for recording and keeping, open questions used, notes checked with the speaker, and no use made of anything an eight-year-old could not have known
Memory is evidence of feeling and of how events were talked about, not of wages, dates or numbers
Nothing remembered is used as proof where the written record is silent

pages.heading: Collection of data: a chronology of the disturbances, May 1938 to 1944
pages.body: The chronology below is the spine of the project: 10 dated entries from the stoppage at Frome to the December 1944 election, each with the place and the source it rests on. Three things become visible when the entries are read in order. The first is speed. The government moved from police action at Frome in the first days of May to announcing a royal commission in August, which is three months, and it was dealing with a labour leader it had detained by the end of May. The second is that the concessions do not arrive all at once: the commission comes in 1938, the labour office and department follow within two years, and the constitution waits until 1944, after the war had changed both the economics of empire and the politics of the people who fought in it. The third is that each entry in the middle of the table sits between a stoppage and an official paper - pressure, then response - which is the pattern the analysis in sections 13 and 14 sets out to explain rather than merely describe. Entries drawn from secondary accounts are marked as such, and no entry rests on an invented source.

pages.heading: Collection of data: extracts from the written sources
pages.body: The extracts below are set out in the four-column form used on the note cards: the source, what it says, what it shows, and how far it can be trusted. Extracts from the real sources are my summaries of what those sources say, with the date and the source given, and not quotations invented to look like the originals: I worked from notes taken in the library, and the one thing a history project must not do is manufacture evidence and then put it in someone else's mouth. Three of the extracts are the most important in the project. The Moyne report matters because it is the government's own commission confirming the wages complaint. The despatches matter because one document contains both of the government's attitudes at once: labour as disorder to be policed, and labour as a question that had to be answered. The Trade Union Law of 1919 matters because it is the legal baseline from which any change must be measured. The fourth extract, from the interview, is INVENTED and labelled: it carries the voice that the real record lacks, and one of its sentences - the remembered wage - is examined and rejected in section 16, which is what makes it useful. Taken together the extracts show the government's position changing from the policing of a dispute to the admission, in an official document, that the dispute had been about something real.

pages.heading: Collection of data: the local sources, and the fact that they are invented
pages.body: This page exists because of a difficulty that every student of this topic meets and most reports hide. The real record of 1938 is an official and newspaper record, and in it the estate labourer appears as a number, a crowd or a problem. A researcher who wants to know what workers wanted has to look for other kinds of evidence: memories, private papers, letters, school and church material. This sample therefore includes four such local sources, and all four are INVENTED: the recorded interview, the estate timekeeper's typed memoir, the 1939 school magazine and the letter signed 'A Cane Farmer's Son'. They are invented because this is a worked example and not a real candidate's submission, and they are labelled as invented everywhere they appear so that nobody can mistake them for evidence about 1938. What they are for is to show the method. Each one is given with its type, when it was written, who wrote it, what that writer wanted, and what it can and cannot support - the same six tests that are applied to the Moyne report. Read that way they divide sharply. The memoir and the letter are single, undated or pseudonymous accounts, useful as leads and unsafe as proof. The school magazine is not much use for what happened in 1938 and is very good evidence of how quickly the events were being rewritten for the young: an editorial of 1939 calls the disturbances 'the unpleasantness of last year' and praises improved conditions. The interview is the most valuable of the four for feeling and the least reliable for fact, and section 16 shows it being tested against the written record rather than believed because it is family.

pages.heading: Collection of data: the legislation and the official record
pages.body: The relationship this project is about can be measured by law, so the legal position at each stage was collected separately from the narrative sources. The starting point is the Trade Union Law of 1919, which took the crime out of combination and left the employer free to ignore a union: it is the legal expression of the pre-1938 relationship, and it explains why a wage dispute could only be pressed by stopping work. The next documents in the table are the products of the pressure that followed: the Moyne Commission's findings, which the British government published in full only in 1945, and the labour office and Labour Department that were set up in Jamaica within two years of the disturbances. The gaps in this table are as important as its entries. Compulsory recognition of unions - a legal duty on an employer to bargain - did not come in the 1940s or indeed for another generation, and no measure of the 1938-44 period in this table touches the ownership of the sugar estates or the price of the crop. That is why the analysis cannot conclude that the workers had won: what the table shows is a government acquiring machinery for dealing with labour, and a constitution acquiring, in 1944, a mass electorate. The last row, the election of December 1944, is the point at which the two changes meet, because the party that formed the government had grown out of the union founded in the year of the disturbances.

pages.heading: Analysis results: the relationship before 1938
pages.body: Before 1938 the relationship between workers and the colonial government was not a bargain, and the evidence shows why it did not need to be. The law of 1919 had removed the criminality of combination, but that was a concession to liberal opinion in Britain rather than a grant of power to Caribbean labour: the returns show that legality without recognition is worth very little to a cane worker who must sell his labour to one estate office in one village. The despatches quoted in Post show the administrative face of the same relationship. When the Governor wrote to London about unrest he described agitators and asked for the means to keep order, and the question of wages entered his letters as a risk to be managed - that wages were too low to live on - rather than as a grievance to be answered. Read that way, the government of 1938 had only two instruments for labour, the police and the commission of inquiry, and it used them in that order. What the evidence does not show is any body of law or administration through which a worker could press a claim without stopping work. That absence is the baseline of the whole project: it is the thing that has to have changed if the answer to the research question is to be yes, and the rest of the analysis measures how far it did.

pages.heading: Analysis: what 1938 changed, and how quickly
pages.body: The disturbances changed the government's method within months, and the speed is one of the more striking things in the evidence. Within days of Frome the response was police; within the month the government had detained a labour leader and then released him as the stoppages spread, which is an admission that the policing instrument had failed; and within three months it had announced a royal commission of its own. By 1939-40 there was a labour officer and a Labour Department, an office that existed because a strike had made it necessary. Each of those steps is a change in how the government dealt with labour, and each was forced by pressure rather than offered. The Moyne Commission's findings then matter in a particular way: the government's own commission confirmed that wages were below what a family needed and attributed the unrest to poverty, poor housing and the absence of any way for workers to be heard. After that document, the government could no longer describe the disturbances as simple disorder, because its own inquiry had said they were an argument. That is a real change in the relationship, and it is the strongest part of the case that 1938 mattered. But the same sources show the limits of the change, and two of them matter more than anything else. The commission recommended improvement inside the colonial system and not a transfer of power, and its report was withheld in full until 1945, which tells you what the government thought of publishing its own findings in wartime. And nothing in the evidence of 1938-40 obliged an employer to sit down with a union. The change, up to that point, was in the government's manners.

pages.heading: Analysis: whose viewpoint is each source, and how far can it be trusted
pages.body: The sources do not merely report the events, they take sides in them, and the analysis has to say so before using them. The Gleaner of 1938 spoke for the literate middle class and its editorials were hostile to the strikers, which is why it is used in this project for what was said and done in public and for the language of the period, and not for the workers' aims. The despatches were written by an official who had to explain himself to London, which makes them excellent evidence of what the government believed and poor evidence of what was actually happening on an estate. The Moyne report is official and self-justifying in its recommendations, and its findings are therefore powerful precisely because they concede the workers' case against the government's interest. The historians have their own commitments: Post reads 1938 as the beginning of decolonisation, Hart wrote as a participant in the politics of the period, and Munroe places the constitutional change at the centre of the story, which is a claim this project accepts only after asking whether the vote changed anything in the cane fields. The bias table below is not an appendix; it is how the evidence in sections 13 and 14 was chosen. Where all the trustworthy sources belong to one side - as they do on the question of what the government did - the project says so and treats the official record as complete on the government's actions and silent on almost everything else.

pages.heading: Analysis: testing the remembered wage against the written record
pages.body: The interview contains one claim of fact - that the wage was about two shillings a day - and the test of a project is what it does with it. Four problems appear as soon as the claim is examined. The speaker was eight years old in 1938 and is recalling what adults said in her hearing, not what she was paid. The detail has passed down a family for nearly ninety years, and numbers are the first thing a story loses. Money changed its value entirely in the intervening decades, so a remembered figure carries no usable meaning without a price index the project does not have. And no real source in the evidence base states a daily rate for Frome in 1938, so there is nothing to test the memory against. What the written record does establish is the substance of the same point, in the government's own words: the Moyne Commission found wages in many places below what a family needed to live on. So the analysis keeps the meaning and discards the number. The remembered figure is recorded on the page where it was collected, marked as unproven, and is not used in the findings as evidence of a wage rate. Two other sentences from the same interview are used, and they are used differently, because they are claims about feeling rather than about fact: the silence in the village after the men came back from Frome, and the change afterwards in how men talked - 'like people who could say no'. A remembered atmosphere cannot be cross-examined, and it is also not the kind of thing a police report would ever record. Used as evidence of how the events were experienced, it is the only such evidence this project has, and it is labelled for what it is.

pages.heading: Discussion: the argument weighed - change in the method of rule, not yet in who held power
pages.body: The evidence supports a narrower answer than the one usually given, and the argument of this project is that between 1938 and 1944 the relationship between workers and the colonial government changed in its method and its language before it changed in the distribution of power. Three pieces of evidence carry the first half of that claim. The government moved from police action to dealing with a labour leader within weeks, from repression to a royal commission within three months, and from no labour administration at all to a labour officer and a Labour Department within two years; and by 1944 the electorate was the mass of the people, with the union's party winning 22 of the 32 elected seats. Those are the changes that make the answer to the research question a clear yes at the level of method. Three pieces of evidence carry the second half. The Moyne report recommended improvement within the colonial system and was withheld in full until 1945, which shows what the government was prepared to let the public know. No measure of the period obliged an employer to recognise a union, so collective bargaining remained a matter of the employer's goodwill, and compulsory recognition was still a generation away. And the ownership of the sugar estates, the price of the crop and the level of the wages that the commission had condemned were all untouched in 1944, when elected members controlled some domestic matters and the Governor and the Colonial Office still stood above them. Put together, the two halves give the finding that the government learned to negotiate because it had to, and that learning to negotiate is not the same as sharing power. The relationship had changed from one in which a worker's grievance was a police matter to one in which a worker's vote was a political fact - which is a great deal, and less than everything.

pages.heading: Findings and conclusion: the research question answered
pages.body: The research question was: How did the 1938 labour disturbances in Jamaica change the relationship between workers and the colonial government? The answer the evidence supports is a qualified yes, and the qualification is the point of the project. Between May 1938 and December 1944 the relationship changed fundamentally in two of the three ways this project set out to measure. In administration, a government that in 1938 had the police and nothing else had by 1940 a labour officer and a Labour Department, and it had moved from arresting a labour leader to negotiating with him, which is a change of method that no amount of later continuity undoes. In politics, the change is even clearer: universal adult suffrage in 1944 and an elected House in which the union's party held 22 of 32 seats put workers inside the political system as voters and as a governing bloc. In the third measure, the law of the workplace, the change was much smaller: unions were lawful in 1919 and employers were still free to ignore them in 1944, so the workers' bargaining power depended on their own organisation and on the goodwill of an employer, and the wages and the estate ownership that the Moyne Commission had condemned were untouched. The relationship therefore changed from one in which labour was a problem of order to one in which labour was a constituency to be courted, and the worker who wanted more than that had to keep organising. The government's own commission supplied the sentence that makes this finding hard to argue with: wages below what a family could live on, attributed to poverty and to the absence of any way for workers to be heard. After 1938 the way to be heard existed. The wage waited longer.

pages.heading: Findings: what further research would settle the questions left open
pages.body: Four questions were left open, and naming them is part of the result rather than a confession of failure. The first is the workers' own voice. No diary, letter or testimony from an estate labourer in 1938 was available to this project, and a researcher with access to the union's early records, the estate papers of the West Indies Sugar Company, or a set of oral histories recorded in the 1970s would be able to test whether the grievances were mainly about wages, as the commission assumed, or about the manner of employment and the power of the estate office, as the interview in this project suggests. The second is what collective bargaining actually did on the estates between 1938 and 1944, which needs the estate books and the union's correspondence and not newspaper reports. The third is the withheld report: the full findings of the Moyne Commission were held back until 1945, and a researcher working in the Colonial Office files could reconstruct what was cut, which would show more precisely how far the government was prepared to admit the truth in wartime. The fourth is comparison: the same question asked of Barbados and Trinidad, where disturbances preceded Jamaica's by a year, would test whether what happened in Jamaica was the local form of a regional change or something made in Jamaica. Each of these would need sources this project could not reach, and each would change part of the answer rather than the whole of it.

pages.heading: Recommendations
pages.body: Four recommendations follow from the project, and each one is something that can actually be done rather than a wish. The first concerns sources, and it is urgent: the people who remember 1938 as children are now in their late nineties, and the material that would answer the first open question - what workers wanted and how the events were experienced - is being lost every year. Schools and libraries should be recording those memories now, with consent, and storing the recordings where students can reach them. The second concerns the teaching of the period. The disturbances are usually taught as a story of heroes and dates, which produces students who can recite 1938 and cannot say what changed; the evidence in this project suggests that the most teachable thing about the year is the gap between the speed of the political change and the slowness of the economic one, and that gap should be the question students are asked about it. The third concerns research access. The newspaper record of 1938 sits on microfilm readers in one or two places in the island, and the Colonial Office files sit in London; digitising the Jamaican newspapers of 1938 and putting the published Moyne report beside them online would move this topic from a project that only a few students can attempt to one that any school can set. The fourth concerns the way the disturbances are named. The official documents of the time called them riots and the newspapers called them an unpleasantness, and a report that repeats that vocabulary without quotation marks has adopted the viewpoint of the people who used the police; the recommendation is small and worth making, that the words of 1938 be quoted rather than borrowed.

pages.heading: Bibliography and note on the invented sources
pages.body: The bibliography is divided in the way the project used the sources: primary material produced at the time or by the institutions involved, secondary works written later, and the local material, every item of which is INVENTED for this worked example. The distinction matters, because a project that mixes a real despatch with an invented memoir in one list has blurred the difference between evidence and illustration. Extracts from the real sources in this report are summaries of what those sources say, with the citation, and are not verbatim quotations.

pages.heading: Acknowledgements
pages.body: Thanks go to the staff of the National Library of Jamaica, who found the 1938 microfilm and showed me how to thread the reader without tearing the film; to the librarian at the parish reference library, who kept the reading room open on a Saturday for the Moyne report; to my great-grandmother, who agreed to be recorded and answered questions about being eight years old in 1938; to the family that lent the estate memoir so that its pages could be photographed, and to the person who allowed its contents to be used; to my teacher, who told me that a project with a thin argument and honest sources is worth more than a confident one with no sources; and to my father, who translated the words my great-grandmother uses for the estate work, which are not in the dictionary.
bullets: The candidate, the school, the family and every local source named in this report are invented for this worked example
The events, dates, legislation and the sources marked [real] are genuine and can be checked in a library or an archive
Extracts from real sources are summaries of what those sources say, with citations, and not invented quotations

examinerNotes: This subject is marked out of 25 in six tasks, and the biggest weight sits in Analysis and Interpretation. This report is built accordingly: five of the 22 sections are analysis, and not one of them narrates the disturbances - the narrative is quarantined in the 10-entry chronology of section 9, where it belongs.

The most advanced thing in the project is its honesty about sources. Every source is labelled by type and origin, the real ones are checkable, the invented local ones are marked INVENTED wherever they appear, and extracts from real sources are given as summaries with citations rather than as manufactured quotations. A marker can see that the candidate understands the difference between evidence and illustration, which is the whole point of the subject.

The source criticism is applied rather than recited. The Gleaner is used for language because it was hostile to the strikers; the Moyne report is used because it is the government's own commission conceding the workers' case; the despatches are read as self-justifying documents; and the historians' commitments - Post's decolonisation frame, Hart's participation, Munroe's focus on the constitution - are named before their evidence is used.

The argument is a real one and it is qualified: the relationship changed in method and in politics between 1938 and 1944, and not in the workplace, because no measure of the period obliged an employer to recognise a union and the wages the Moyne report condemned were untouched when the first elected House met. The report reaches a verdict on each claim rather than asserting the usual story.

The strongest single piece of technique is section 16, where the one factual claim in the oral testimony - a remembered wage - is examined against the written record, found untestable, recorded where it was collected, marked UNPROVEN and left out of the findings, while the same interview's statements about fear and dignity are used as the evidence they can be. Candidate, centre, family and all local sources are invented placeholders; the history is not. Run your own project on your own question.
